name: Digital Twins for Experiments
title: Digital Twins for Experiments
answer: Digital twins for experiments are computational models that mirror a physical experimental system, its instruments, samples, and protocols, so that a planned procedure can be simulated before it is run on real equipment. They cover wet lab and dry lab workflows, from liquid handling and spectroscopy to cell culture and materials synthesis, and they include both the equipment state and the expected data output. In laboratory automation, a twin may represent a specific robot, plate reader, or reactor, along with its calibration and maintenance history. The scope also extends to virtual commissioning of new protocols and to training operators on rare or hazardous procedures.

They cover wet lab and dry lab workflows, from liquid handling and spectroscopy to cell culture and materials synthesis, and they include both the equipment state and the expected data output. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A digital twin for an experiment typically runs on standard laboratory computing resources, often a workstation or a small server with a GPU if the model includes physics or learned components. It connects to instrument control software, electronic lab notebooks, and laboratory information management systems through APIs or file exchange. The twin itself is usually built from a combination of physics based simulators, discrete event models of the workflow, and sometimes a learned surrogate model that approximates a slower high fidelity simulation. Data from sensors and logs is streamed or batch loaded to keep the twin aligned with the physical system.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by defining the experimental system as a set of state variables, such as temperatures, volumes, positions, and instrument settings, and the transitions between them. A model is then fitted or configured so that its outputs match historical runs or known physical behavior, a step called calibration or history matching. When a new protocol is proposed, it is executed against the twin first, and the simulated results are compared with acceptance criteria before the real experiment is authorized. Discrepancies between twin predictions and actual outcomes are recorded and used to update the model, which is a form of continuous validation rather than a one time build.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around experimental digital twins center on data provenance, model validity, and the consequences of acting on a simulation that may be wrong. The twin inherits the access controls of the underlying instrument data and lab records, so ownership and confidentiality follow the same policies as the physical experiment. A key risk is silent drift, where the twin becomes less accurate as equipment wears or reagents change, and no one notices until a real run fails. Provenance requires recording which version of the twin, which calibration data, and which assumptions were used for each simulated result, so that a decision can be audited later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Digital twins for experiments are moving toward closed loop operation, where the twin proposes the next experiment, the robot runs it, and the result is fed back to update the twin automatically. This is sometimes called self driving laboratory or autonomous experimentation, and it depends on reliable uncertainty estimates from the twin so that the system knows when to ask a human. Another direction is federated twins, where several labs share a common model of an instrument or protocol without sharing raw data, which could speed up method transfer. The practical limit remains the cost of building and maintaining a twin that is accurate enough to replace a real pilot run.
